snippet.title: Use Grok Bot Better Than 99% of People (Full Course)
snippet.description:
I sit down with Ras Mic to see how he runs his work and his life through Grok Bot. He calls himself a Grok Bot maxi, and he uses it as a personal agent and as an orchestrator that hands engineering work to Claude Code. He walks me through five areas: engineering, design, content ideation, business and finance, and shopping. Along the way he shows his bots, his prompts, and the projects they shipped, including Pluto, Bezalel, a Rust trading app, and a Shopify store for his brother's clothing brand. If you ship ideas, this episode gives you a setup you can copy today.

Timestamps

00:00 – Intro
01:55 – Engineering Bot
07:57 – Why use Grok Bot as an Orchestrator
14:01 – Grok Bot + Claude Code
19:43 – Security Checks
21:54 – Designer Bot
31:12 – Content Bot
37:19 – Business & Finance Bot
42:41 – Shopping Bot
44:53 – Closing Thoughts

Key Points

• Give each serious project its own bot, keep one general engineering bot for random ideas, and delete bots once they stop being useful.
• Use Grok Bot to orchestrate and Claude Code with Opus 5.5 to write the code.
• Ras Mic says the $200-a-month Claude Code plan is worth $8,000 to $12,000 in API credits, so he leans on subscriptions.
• Lock the design in Paper before any code gets written, with a design system the agent can reference.
• A YouTube bot scans X at 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. and sends three video topics with tweets, title ideas, and resources.
• Finance bots connected through Plaid give Ras Mic's advisor bot enough context to talk him out of shiny objects.

Numbered Section Summaries

1. Engineering Bot

Grok Bot organizes work into bots, each with its own context, skills, and computer, where the ChatGPT app gives you threads that get mixed up. Ras Mic lets context decide. Pluto, his Bible app, and Bezalel (at $200 MRR) each get a bot, a general engineering bot catches random ideas like Still, a screenshot extension built in two prompts, and permanent bots handle IT and ML. When a bot stops being useful, he right-clicks and deletes it.

2. Grok Bot Orchestrates, Claude Code Builds 

Ras Mic sends ideas to his engineering bot at night and wakes up to a repo on GitHub, like the AI governance compliance app it built after a friend told him about government contracting. For Pluto, he had Grok Bot review a plan from a PDF, revise it with his feedback and a friend's, then build it with Claude Code on Opus 5.5 using /goal. The run went for hours and returned five working PRs, which people are now testing.

3. Why Grok Bot + Claude Code 

I ask why an engineer would put Grok Bot on top of Claude Code or Codex, and Ras Mic points to the UX. He works through PRs from his phone during dinner at his mom's house and talks to a bot on speaker while he drives. Grok Bot also covers the business side. While building VP Cloud, a Canadian sovereign cloud, one of his bots emailed a GPU provider on its own to ask for a discount and mentioned his YouTube subscriber count.

5. Design Bot

Ras Mic collects inspiration from X and Mobbin, sends a screenshot to his agent, and has it build a design system in Paper through the Paper MCP. He used that flow for his brother's clothing brand, where Grok Bot designed a Christian gothic storefront in Paper and then built it as a Shopify front end. 

6. Content Bot 

Twice a day, at 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., Ras Mic's YouTube bot scans X and sends three topics that fit his channel, each with source tweets, a title idea, and resources. He mostly scripts his own videos because people prefer people, and he uses an editor bot to explore styles and brief his human editor.

7. Advisor Bot

Ras Mic has shiny object syndrome, so he runs ideas past an advisor bot. His finance bots connect to his accounts through Plaid, so the advisor can read his transactions and hold him to his goals. When he sent it a real estate listing, it advised against buying, citing cash pulled from his other goals, a seller who wanted unrepresented buyers only, and a boiler and furnace from 2009.

8. Shopper Bot

Grok Bot scans eBay every day for sealed GPUs. For Ras's PS5 Pro, it emailed the seller, learned it was a store in Ontario two hours away, gave him the number to call, and bought the console once he confirmed. It also found shoes for his sciatica and emailed the list to his wife for approval.

snippet.title: Claude Fable 5.2: How I’d Make Money With It
snippet.description:
In this solo episode, I share 12 prompts for Fable 5.2 across four areas: making money, productivity, video and content, and hardware. I run several of them live, including an audit of my design agency, a freelance job Fable 5.2 found on Upwork, a 100-niche research sweep with subagents, and a minimalist phone it designed from one prompt. I cover why Fable 5.2 can work 10 to 12 hours on its own, why it now admits when it lacks an answer, and how to sell results as a fixed-price service. If you want to make money, get more done, or build hardware with Fable 5.2, this episode gives you prompts you can copy today.

Timestamps

00:00 – Intro
01:00 – Prompt 1: Audit Your Entire Business
02:05 – Prompt 2: A Freelance Job End to End
03:46 – Prompt 3: A Hundred Niches at Once
04:33 – Prompt 4: Rebuild the Ancient Software
05:25 – Prompt 5: Deal Checker for a Boring Business
06:54 – Results from Prompts
08:53 – Prompt 6: Grill Me
09:33 – Prompt 7: Operate Legacy Apps
10:07 – Prompt 8: Red Team My Plan
11:11 – Video and Marketing Engineering
12:39 – Prompt 9: Short-Form Editor
13:05 – Prompt 10: Niche Explainer Videos
13:24 – Prompt 11: One Episode, Every Format
13:56 – Prompt 12: One person Hardware Company
16:42 – A Minimalist Phone Idea
17:41 – Design and Mockups
18:31 – Closing Thoughts

Key Points

• Fable 5.2 works 10 to 12 hours on its own, so I hand it jobs that take a high-end consultant a week.
• Freelance jobs and software rebuilds can now sell per output, where people used to bill by the hour.
• Stronger subagents let me research 100 niches in one prompt and get back one ranked table.
• Fable 5.2 now admits uncertainty, which opens up finance and legal work like checking a seller's P&L.
• Videos at $1 to $5 each let me build faceless channels and own distribution.
• One prompt gets me a parts list, circuit design, firmware, and a printable enclosure for a device.

Numbered Section Summaries

1. Long Jobs and Freelance Work 

My audit prompt asks Fable 5.2 to review my website, pricing, onboarding, emails, and top five competitors, keep a running log, and rank the 10 changes most likely to make money, with evidence for each. For LCA, my design agency, it ranked every call with evidence and stayed to the point, as it has on every business we incubate. I asked it to find a freelance job it could do, and it picked an Upwork equity analyst report on TDMX at a $450 fixed price

2. Subagents and Old Software 

Fable 5.2 runs many subagents well, so one prompt spins up a subagent for each of 100 niches to find the top three complaints, what people pay today, and how hard each niche is to reach, then returns one ranked table and the five to build for. Another prompt hands it a spreadsheet a client has run their business on for 12 years and asks it to figure out what the sheet does, rebuild it as a simple web app

3. A Model That Admits Uncertainty 

Hallucination has held legal and finance teams back from AI, and Fable 5.2 now admits when it lacks an answer, the way a person would. My deal checker prompt hands it a seller's P&L and listing, asks it to flag everything that fails to add up, label each number verified, unverified, or suspicious, and write the 15 questions I should ask before making an offer.

4. Productivity Prompts 

The Grill Me prompt interviews me with 20 questions, one at a time, about how I make decisions in my business, then turns my answers into a skill file Fable 5.2 follows from then on. It operates a computer well, so it can open an old invoicing app, export last month's invoices, match them against the bank statement, list outstanding ones, and check with me before sending anything.

5. Video, Content, and Distribution 

My three prompts cut a raw four-minute talking-head video to its strongest 45 seconds with three hooks, build a 60-second animated niche explainer with five opening lines, and turn one transcript into a PDF playbook, five tweets in my voice, a newsletter, a two-minute free tool, and flags on any claim that needs a check.

6. Vibe Manufacturing From One Prompt 

I recall Anthropic saying in a blog post that Fable 5.2 designed three working devices from a single prompt, so my hardware prompt asks for a one-job device for one niche with a priced parts list, circuit design, firmware, a printable enclosure, and the cost to make 100.

snippet.title: AI Agents are too good at marketing now
snippet.description:
I sit down with Cody Schneider, to break down how to become a top 0.1% marketer with GrokBot, Claude Code, and the tools around them. Cody shows the environment an agent needs to do marketing work: data in a warehouse, write access to ad platforms, and API tools for images, video, and leads. We build static ads live for Idea Browser, Late Checkout, Cursor, and more, then make a UGC avatar video ad with motion graphics for about $5. I add two pieces of my own: a swipe warehouse of creative references and a creative director agent that scores every ad. If you build products and hear crickets, this episode gives you workflows you can set up today.

Timestamps

00:00 – Intro
04:29 – Agents are now Marketers
09:56 – Data Pipelines & Warehouses
13:56 – Getting your agent access to data
16:15 – The tools for your agent
18:08 – Agents become.1% marketers
20:43 – Swipe Warehouse and Context
22:35 – Creating Static Ads
29:08 – Static Ads Results
30:03 – Creating UGC Avatar Ads
36:28 – Running the Workflow
37:58 – UGC Ad Results
39:51 – Human Creators Through Tribe and Sideshift
41:42 – Reviewing the Static Ads
43:29 – The role of Creative Director
50:49 – Closing Thoughts

Links Mentioned: 

Cody's Marketing Skills: https://startup-ideas-pod.link/cody-marketing-skills
Guide for setting up Facebook Developer Token: https://startup-ideas-pod.link/Facebook-ads-developer-token-setup

Key Points

• Agents do marketing's middle work once they have data, platform access, and tools.
• A data pipeline into a warehouse gives agents full-funnel data and keeps them off rate-limited APIs.
• Agents write to Facebook and Google Ads through their APIs and read data only from the warehouse.
• One skill turns a brand URL into five researched, on-brand static ads.
• A UGC avatar ad with motion graphics costs about $5, compared with $300 to $500 from humans.
• Creative velocity wins, since Facebook's algorithm matches good creative to the right buyer.

Numbered Section Summaries

1. Agents are now Marketers

Cody says a static ad used to need a graphic designer and a copywriter, and a UGC video needed a creator, a video editor, and a motion graphics designer. Now GrokBot, Claude Code, or Dots handles that work with code and tokens, and Mirage Tesseract one-shot edits a 90-minute podcast, cutting silence and retakes and tracking the active speaker. I see the job of anyone building a business in 2027 as building the system around these agents, and Cody compares that role to a conductor, or a StarCraft player coordinating swarms.

2. Giving Agents the Data 

Cody warns that agents querying ad APIs directly flood their context, hallucinate, or build their own local database full of duplicates. He uses Airbyte as a data pipeline from Facebook Ads, Google Analytics, HubSpot, and the payment processor into a ClickHouse data warehouse, a Graft partner. With everything in one place, the agent queries as often as it likes and ties an ad all the way to revenue and customer lifetime value.

3. Tools for Agents

The third piece is tools: Kai AI for images and video, FAL for transcription, OpenRouter for LLMs, and Git Leads or Apollo for email and person data. With these, Cody's Google Ads agent checks in real time whether each search term carries buyer intent for its landing page, auditing 5,000 terms in 20 seconds. Graft bundles the data, access, and tools, with a free start and multiplayer access for teams, and the open source route works too.

snippet.title: 8 Businesses for the AI Age
snippet.description:
In this solo episode, I lay out how I think about building an AI-proof business now that anyone can press a few buttons and spin up a company in seconds. Layoffs keep coming, people copy products pixel for pixel, and I still see more opportunity than ever. I walk through eight categories: atoms, permission, attention, timing, belonging, liquidity, unique data, and outcomes. I share examples like Hampton, final.com, and Cars & Bids, say how I'd rank the categories, and show how to mix them. If you're an employee looking at a startup or a founder worried about getting copied, this episode gives you a map for building something with value when AI makes software, content, and answers almost free.

Timestamps

00:00 – Intro
01:17 – Atoms: Physical Businesses
02:26 – Permission: Licenses, Regulation, and Partnerships
04:10 – Attention: Building a Media Machine
06:28 – Timing: Spotting Trends Early
08:24 – Belonging: Paid Communities and IRL Events
10:59 – Liquidity: Marketplaces
14:38 – Unique Data: Data Brokers and Curated Directories
18:31 – Outcomes: Customers Paying for Results
20:44 – Closing Thoughts

Key Points

• Physical businesses hold up against overnight clones, and I expect their valuations to rise as tech money moves in.
• Licenses, regulation, and preferred-vendor deals are permission that a copycat has a hard time getting on day one.
• Media is underrated, and AI lets you run a content machine around a micro niche.
• A first mover's product may be easy to copy, while the data, brand, and trust it collects stay AI-proof.
• Marketplaces rank among the stickiest businesses of all time, and agents let a team of one to five run one.

Section Summaries

1. Atoms and Permission 

Pixels are software businesses and atoms are physical ones, like a coffee shop or the plumber who fixes your clogged toilet. They're harder to run, they hold up against overnight clones, and I think their valuations go up once AI and tech money spots the moat. Permission covers licenses, regulation, and deals, so you could partner with a lawyer and handle marketing, growth, and AI while they run the firm.

3. Attention 

Attention is somehow underrated right now, and people follow people. I used to hate making short form video, and now Opus 5.5 is my editor, I create on my own schedule, and I got hundreds of thousands of views in the last week. I'd pick a micro niche and build a media company around it with newsletters, meme pages, or founder-led content, aiming for a trustworthy brand that people come to for that niche.

4. Timing 

I see more trends in more micro niches than ever, and sometimes I'm shocked by how few people have built for them. I'd use ideabrowser.com, GrokBot, Claude Duet, or any personal agent platform to monitor your niches, then build first, whether that's software, a physical product, or a media company. 

5. Belonging 

People are as connected as ever and feel as disconnected as ever, so I see a big opportunity in paid communities built around a shared goal, like a Circle or Skool group or a weekly virtual event that keeps people accountable. We threw an IRL event in Nashville last week for founders deploying agents, and demand ran past what we knew how to meet.

6. Liquidity 

People tell me software is done, and marketplaces are the example I give back. A friend of mine launched final.com, I think last week, where you bid every week on curated high-end collectible cars, and he markets it to his big Instagram audience, while Cars & Bids sold for many millions of dollars.

You see data brokers making millions of dollars a week, and platforms like, I think, Mercor and micro1 got coding data and sold it to the big models, which stay hungry for new types of data. Customers are starting to pay for results through automated AI services, like a creative agency that makes logos and landing pages on the fly or a machine that studies Fiverr and Upwork and bids on the work. snippet.title: The $1M+ Solo Grok Bot Business (Full Course)
snippet.description:
I sit down with Nick, co-founder of Orgo, to break down how to build a custom Grok Bot for a business and sell it for $25,000 up front with a $3,000-a-month retainer. Nick demos Bops, the agent platform he built in a 36-hour weekend, where each bot has its own phone number, email, and computer with four screens. He walks me through his research, design, and build process, the stack behind each bot, and the offer he takes to business owners. We also cover how to pick a niche by calling 50 people you know and how to turn one free case study into warm referrals. If you want to sell AI employees to businesses, this episode gives you the stack, the offer, and an open source repo you can fork today.

Timestamps

Key Points

• Busy owners want their problems solved, so a GrokBot built for their industry wins over a platform they have to set up.
• Nick builds in three steps: research the category, design in Paper, then pick a stack and read the docs.
• Each bot gets its own email, phone number, computer, and connectors through Agent Mail, Agent Phone, Orgo, and Composio.
• The SMB offer is $25,000 up front for a system the owner keeps, plus an optional $3,000-a-month retainer.
• A free website redesign, a money-back guarantee, and free lead magnets make the offer easy to accept.
• Call 50 people you know, do the first build free, and trade the case study for warm intros.

Numbered Section Summaries

1. Why Businesses Want a Custom GrokBot 

Nick built Bops, short for business ops, as a GrokBot clone in a weekend, and his demo video got 75K views on Twitter. I see the price of software trending toward zero, with the money in upselling agents and human intelligence, and Nick sees purpose-built apps for one business taking off. Owners are too busy to set up GrokBot or Dots themselves, so Nick ships agents pre-built for an industry like insurance or dental clinics, each with its own phone number, email, and Slack connector.

2. Research, Design, Build 

Nick built Bops in one long-running T3 Code thread with Opus 5.5 over 36 hours, with loops running overnight. He starts by having the model research GrokBot, Meta's Muse, and OpenAI's Dots, then designs in Paper through the Paper MCP, asking for three or four variations and combining the best parts, a process he calls diverge and then converge. He tried T3 Code after seeing Theo's content on Twitter and likes that it is simple, free, and works with a Claude subscription.

3. The Stack Behind Each Bot 

Orgo provides each bot's computer, Agent Mail its email, Agent Phone its phone number, and Composio its connectors through one API connection. For every feature, Nick tells his agent to read the docs and the API references, then sends CleanShot screenshots of bugs or of GrokBot UI elements he likes, and I keep a swipe file of references for the same job. Bops gives each bot a full computer for privacy and multitasking, where GrokBot gives each bot a screen, and Nick hosts on Orgo, Fly, or Vercel and ships fast.

4. The $25,000 Offer 

For SMBs, Nick sells the system for $25,000 up front, maybe collected in two halves, then offers an optional $3,000-a-month retainer after a 30-day implementation. When I play a dental clinic owner and ask about the return, Nick compares one bot to a front desk hire at $50,000 to $70,000 a year, out of 15 bots the owner keeps. Owners like owning the system over feeling held by the neck on a retainer for AI employees.

8. Landing the First Clients 

Nick suggests calling 50 people you know who run a business or work high up in one, then doing the first build free for a case study, which is how he found the promotional products industry. Shadow that first client while they share their screen on manual work like invoices, and the right agents become clear. I'd frame the free build as a $50,000-a-year service and ask for intros to three local peers in return

snippet.title: SaaS is dead?
snippet.description:
In this solo episode, I explain why I say SaaS is dead and what I see taking its place. For 15 years, SaaS meant paying engineers to build a tool and charging per seat, and now models like Opus 5.5, GPT-6, and Argon make the tool easy to build. I walk through what I call smart SaaS: give the tool away for free, collect data and network effects, and make money by upselling AI agents and human services. I share a calorie tracking example, three ways to charge, and why enterprises still pay per seat. If you build software, this episode gives you a map for building something people want in a market where the tool is free.

Timestamps
00:00 – Intro
00:47 – SaaS 1.0
02:56 – SaaS 2.0: The New Business Model
05:12 – How to monetize SaaS 2.0
06:18 – Service is the new Software
07:22 – SaaS Is Dead, Long Live SaaS
08:58 – SMB vs Enterprise
10:31 – Closing Thoughts

Key Points

• AI makes the tool easy to build, so the per-seat model of the last 15 years has run its course.
• Smart SaaS gives the tool away and collects data and network effects as payment.
• The money comes from upselling intelligence from AI agents and services from humans.
• Agents can charge by token or by outcome, and human services by the week or month.
• SaaS for SMBs, prosumers, and individuals trends toward free, while enterprises still pay something per seat.
• The market for getting things done is bigger than the market for tools, so the total market for SaaS grows.

Numbered Section Summaries

1. How SaaS Worked 

For the last 15 years, the hard part of SaaS was getting enough smart engineers in a room to code a high-quality tool for a human to use. Customers paid per seat, at prices like $9.99 or $29.99, to use that tool in the cloud. The model made people billions of dollars, and Slack, which I believe sold for $29 billion, shows how well it worked.

2. AI Makes the Tool Easy 

Models at the level of Opus 5.5, GPT-6, Astra, Argon, and Carbon make building the software easy. One or two people with AI can now build what used to take a team of 20, so charging per seat for a tool stops working.

3. Give the Tool Away 

In smart SaaS, I still build a tool, and I give it away for free: the CRM, the dashboard, the app. I look for niches where people pay for a tool in the old model and hand them that tool at zero cost. Users pay with data, which I can sell or use to make the tool better, and with network effects that build a moat.

4. Upselling Intelligence 

I call the old model dumb SaaS because it is only a tool, and the new model smart SaaS because it is intelligent. With a free CRM, I charge when the customer wants AI agents to do work in it, or I upsell a service delivered by humans, which lines up with Sequoia's view of trillion-dollar services as the new software. A calorie tracking app can give away the tracker, charge for agents that build personalized meal plans or track calories more precisely, and sell a weekly weight coach.

5. A Product Studio of Free Tools 

Per-seat pricing limited the market, since only some people want to pay for tools. I see a product studio built around free tools, with upsells to agents or humans, as a way into the many niches that are wide open right now. That is why I say SaaS is dead, long live SaaS.

6. Pricing Agents and Services 

Agents can charge by token or by outcome, so the customer pays when the agents complete the work. Human services can charge a weekly or monthly fee. The market for people accomplishing things is bigger than the market for people using a tool, so I see the total market for SaaS growing.

7. Where Enterprises Fit 

SaaS for SMBs, prosumers, and individuals trends toward free. Fortune 500 and Fortune 2000 companies may still pay something per seat, a number I expect to drop over time, plus upsells to humans and superintelligence. Some enterprises want to pay for the security and for the feeling of being taken care of.

snippet.title: $100M ARR Founder: The Next Big AI Opportunity
snippet.description:
I sit down with Jon Noronha, co-founder and chief product officer of Gamma, to break down agent harnesses and the startup openings around them. Jon explains how Gamma rebuilt its product as a creative agent this year and walks me through the roughly 20 models and 200 calls behind one finished presentation. We talk about AI smell, why taste carries more weight than evals in creative work, how Gamma tests a new model within the hour, and the fast mode test that lost to good friction. Jon also shares the harnesses he wants to see, from a Slack agent that learns his voice to a couch shopping tool that checks the fit in your room. If you want to build a vertical agent, this episode gives you a clear model of what a harness is and where your edge can come from.

This episode was made possible thanks to Anthropic (the team behind Claude) for hosting us at Claude Founder house and sponsoring the episode.

Timestamps

00:00 – Intro
01:23 – What Is an Agent Harness
03:36 – Harnesses as the New Wrappers
04:25 – Inside One Gamma Prompt
08:23 – Where Vertical Harnesses Fit
11:08 – Finding Your Edge
11:56 – Opportunities for Harnesses
13:09 – Designing a Niche Harness
13:48 – AI Smell
15:49 – Evals and Taste
18:40 – Who Pays for AI
19:44 – The Gamma for X
20:19 – A Harness for Slack
22:01 – Building on Other People's Models
23:28 – Closed vs. Open Source Models
24:11 – A Broad but Shallow Stack
24:57 – Prompts vs. Fine-Tuning
25:30 – Testing New Models
26:25 – Running Experiments
29:10 – The Marketing Engineer
32:26 – Interesting Automations
33:33 – The Top 1% Marketing Engineer
35:00 – Everyone Is Now a VP of Agents
36:19 – Experiments as a Numbers Game
38:26 – Underhyped: AI Image Models
40:42 – Startup Opportunities
45:40 – What Jon Would Build Next
47:26 – Closing Thoughts

Key Points

• An agent harness is the set of tools an agent uses to act, check its own work, and deliver a finished result.
• One Gamma presentation uses about 20 models and 200 calls, including rounds of visual QA.
• Strong harness ideas sit in subjective work, where people care about the output and want a human in the loop.
• Your edge comes from a distinct vision, proprietary data, or a business that mixes AI with the physical world.
• Gamma gets 98% of its value from prompts and treats fine-tuning as a cost and quality optimization.
• Experiments reward volume, and Gamma's fast mode test showed that good friction raised paid conversion.

Numbered Section Summaries

1. What is an Agent Harness 

Gamma started in 2020, took off in 2023, and spent this year rebuilding its product from preset LLM workflows into an agent. Jon defines the harness as the tools an agent uses to act in its environment, inspect its own work, and ask the user for preferences, with Claude Code as the best-known example for programming. I call harnesses the new wrappers, and Jon agrees, since the wrapping is most of the work and even OpenAI and Anthropic put heavy effort into harness development.

2. Inside One Gamma Prompt 

When someone pastes messy notes and asks for 20 slides, Gamma spins up a cloud sandbox, asks a few questions through a form, and pulls context from Notion, Slack, or Linear. It writes an outline, picks a template with vision models and embedding search, then generates text, layouts, images, and charts in parallel in about a minute. A vision model checks every slide for misaligned text, cropped heads, and weak contrast, and after rounds of fixes the deck has used about 20 models and 200 calls.

3. Where Vertical Harnesses Fit 

Jon looks for problems that differ from coding: subjective work where people disagree on what good looks like and care about the specifics of the output. Jon calls AI image models underhyped, since most people use them for menus and logos while Gamma uses about 10 image models for diagrams, textures, and icons. Numbered Section Summaries

1. Why James Sells to Main Street 

James started out owning agencies for local businesses and startups, running performance ads, social, and SEO. He owns Diesel Dudes, a mobile diesel repair business in Charlotte that dispatches mechanics to broken-down semi trucks, and he grew it with ads, funnels, and local SEO. He packages that experience into how he'd start an agency again today.

2. The Market and the Niches 

Roughly 112,000 plumbing and HVAC companies average about $2.5 million a year, only 14% of owners say AI is fully part of how they run, and they pay around $129 per lead. James steers toward urgent, high-ticket work like commercial hood cleaning, dental implants, tree services, irrigation, sport courts, artificial turf, chimney sweeping, gutter guards, septic, crawl space, and backup generators. I'd add snow removal in the Northeast, since the trades around where you live are your unfair advantage.

3. Funnels as the Offer 

Agencies still charge $20,000 for a good funnel, and anyone who knows a coding agent can build one fast at high quality. For an HVAC company, James tests a free check, a $79 tune-up tripwire, an instant price, a repair-or-replace quiz, an owner video sales letter, and an advertorial, each tied to its own ad campaign. A tripwire liquidates ad spend: at $1 a click, 20 visitors cost $20, one $20 sale covers it, and the rest leave an email address.

4. Pricing, Proof, and Mindset 

A plumber with 100 leads a month at $129 spends about $13,000, and one $1,714 job pays for 13 of those leads. James suggests an intro install plus monthly testing and reporting, possibly performance pricing later, and a first free build in exchange for a case study. I believe you have to commit to being the best person to help plumbers in Dallas for six to 18 months, and James recommends one market and one geography for six months.

snippet.title: The 9 Stages of AI Agent Adoption, Explained
snippet.description:
In this solo episode, I break down the war on AI agents, from Amazon blocking Meta's Muse to Delta treating outside booking agents as unauthorized automated activity to Yelp charging agents for access. I share how I think about an agent, as a customer with a credit card who reads your site instead of looking at it, and the ladder of trust that runs from research to prepare to pay. Then I walk through each big player's bet, my nine stages for how this war plays out, five moves any business can make this week, and the startup ideas I see between agents and the businesses they buy from. If you run a store or build products, this episode gives you a map for selling to customers who send an agent to shop for them.

Timestamps

00:00 – Intro
02:09 –The Three Camps
05:08 – How I Define an Agent
06:52 – The Ladder of Trust
08:54 – Real Reasons to Block Agents
09:48 – What Agents Skip
12:57 – How Each Company is Playing it
17:06 – Lessons From Mint and Plaid
17:49 – The 9 stages of The War on Agents
21:56 – What to do this week
24:39 – Startup Idea 1: Agent Readiness
25:48 – Startup Idea 2: Plaid for One Vertical
26:22 – Startup Idea 3: Insurance for Agents
26:57 – Startup Idea 4: Analytics for Agent Traffic
27:26 – Startup Idea 4: Agent Specialist
28:05 – Closing Thoughts

Key Points

• Agents read product details, prices, shipping, and return policies, so plain-text facts on the page decide whether they pick you.
• Agents climb a ladder of trust from research to prepare to pay, and the whole fight happens on the pay rung.
• Many blocks protect the ad and upsell revenue that agents skip on the way to the sale.
• The biggest stores block, the biggest audiences open the door, and payment and security companies want the toll booth.
• I expect a Plaid moment for agent identity and payments, followed later by ads that buy an agent's first recommendation.
• Vertical Plaids, agent insurance, and agent analytics are open lanes for startups right now.

Numbered Section Summaries

1. Who Blocks and Who Welcomes 

Amazon started blocking Meta's Muse agent around September, Delta treats outside booking agents as unauthorized automated activity, and Yelp lets agents in only through its paid data licensing program. In the middle, Zillow welcomes agents acting for real customers while its anti-scraping tools sometimes stop them, and Walmart, a Muse partner, called its Muse failures an accident. On the welcoming side, Meta works with Walmart and Stripe on an open standard, Shopify lets merchants sell through AI channels, and Visa and Mastercard build ways to recognize trusted agents.

2. A Customer Who Reads Instead of Looks 

I think of an agent as a customer with a credit card who reads instead of looks. It skips your $100,000 homepage video, banners, and countdown pop-ups, and it reads your product details, prices, shipping costs, and return policy. When I ask my agent to find a replacement air purifier filter, compare delivered prices, and check with me before buying anything over $50, I give it a goal, rules, and a limit.

3. The Ladder of Trust 

Agents climb three rungs: research, prepare, and pay. Most companies accept the first rung because it works like search, and the whole war happens on the third, so I see businesses making a mistake when they block all three. An agent compares five suppliers in the time it takes me to open one tab and stays loyal to whatever worked last time, so a stuck checkout quietly sends it to a competitor.

4. Why Companies Block 

Some reasons to block hold up, since an agent might place 50 orders instead of five, the customer calls the store about it, and an airline has to prove you authorized a booking. Money drives a lot of it, because Amazon earns tens of billions a year from ads and airlines profit from seat upgrades, bags, and credit card offers that agents skip. Amazon and Delta also build their own agents

5. The 9 Stages

Banks fought Mint.com until Plaid built a proper connection between apps and banks, and the banks moved from blocking to signing deals to charging for access. I see agents on that same path, from blocking today to an arms race to a split where sales businesses let agents in, data businesses charge, and giants build their own, then a Plaid moment for agent identity and payments. After that, welcoming companies win customers, everyone competes for agents with faster checkouts and pages written for agents, ads come back to buy an agent's first recommendation

snippet.title: Meta Muse Will Create 1,000 Millionaires
snippet.description:

In this solo episode, I break down how to make money with Meta Muse by mining Facebook groups, Marketplace, and Instagram to match buyers with sellers. The idea came after my wife and I had a baby and the agency we hired for a night nurse admitted it found candidates in Facebook groups. I demo Muse finding night nurses at $30 an hour in Montreal, show how to give it a phone number through Bland AI, and share the Marketplace and Instagram tactics I'd use. I close with my four-level framework for growing a matching side business into a trusted list, a community, and a vertical software company.

01:19 – Sponsor: Brex

05:44 – Owning the asset and data

21:40– Goods vs. Services
22:15 – Muse vs. Dots and Instinct
24:09 – Closing Thoughts

Key Points

• Muse mines public Facebook groups, Marketplace, and Instagram to match buyers and sellers in any niche and city.
• A clean list of names, needs, prices, and trust signals is an asset I own and can sell later.
• Facebook groups, business pages, and IG niche pages look undervalued as Muse agents start crawling them.
• I tell Muse where to look, and Facebook groups gave me the highest quality data.
• My four levels: mine the data, own the list, own the room, then build technology.
• A lean cost structure lets me charge a success fee of a few hundred dollars and keep high margins.

Numbered Section Summaries

1. The Night Nurse Search 

My wife and I recently had a baby, and our search for a night nurse led us to an agency. The agency admitted it searched Facebook groups for Miami, South Florida, and New York night nurses, and I realized Muse can do that work today. I expect a thousand-plus millionaires to come out of this era.

2. Matching Buyers and Sellers 

Billions of people post needs and offers in Facebook groups, on Marketplace, and on Instagram. I pick a niche, a city, and rules for who I approve, like night nurses in Orlando, and Muse handles the structure, matching, DMs, calls, texts, and booking. The top eBay sellers made millions by finding unique products to sell, and connecting buyer and seller holds the same value here.

3. Clean Data as an Asset 

Posts across these platforms vary in quality, so Muse cleans the data into Airtable, Google Sheets, or whatever I use. That list of names, needs, prices, and trust signals compounds into an asset I own and can sell, and I'll cover data brokering in a future episode. Each niche needs its own cleaning approach, starting with what my ICP wants.

4. A Phone Line and Undervalued Pages 

People give Muse a dedicated number through Bland AI's Agent Line, a non-VoIP US number with talk and text that I believe costs about $15, so Muse can get a number, call me, reach out to people, and close sales. Facebook groups have about 1.8 billion monthly active users by my estimate, and with millions of Muse agents crawling them, I'd start a group, a business page like a Miami agency for night nurses, or an IG niche page now. Buying Facebook groups may also be an arbitrage, so check Facebook's terms of service first.

5. The Four Levels 

Level one is mining other people's groups, Marketplace, and IG, and level two is owning a cleaned, priced, trusted list off platform. Level three is owning the room through your own Facebook group, IG niche page, or Marketplace storefront, and level four is building technology like SaaS, vertical agents, and vertical harnesses that automate the workflow end to end. Muse also works as my content hub for Instagram research, and its lean cost structure lets me charge parents a few hundred dollars where an agency team might have charged thousands.

In this solo episode, I share what I learned after a week with Gemini 4 Argon, Google's new frontier model. I show three places it shines: marketing with AI, physical AI, and complex engineering, with a real build for each. You'll see Argon rebuild my holding company's website, write a post in my voice, design a Shopify product customizer that exports STL files, and build a free quoting app for commercial cleaning companies. • Argon gets the engineering right on prompt one, and design takes a few more rounds.
• /plan, /subagents, and /goal give me the biggest jumps in output quality.

Numbered Section Summaries

1. Where Argon Stands 

After a week of testing, I see three strengths in Gemini 4 Argon: marketing with AI, physical AI, and complex engineering. Google now has a frontier-level model backed by a huge amount of data. I prefer other harnesses to Antigravity today and expect Google to catch up, and Argon also runs in Cursor and OpenCode.

2. Marketing With AI 

In 2021 my team spent 40,000 hours on the Late Checkout holding company website, which cost us around $200,000, and the business has brought in more than $40 million in revenue. I asked Argon for a better version in a Mondrian style, and it added cars, movement, a world passport, sounds, and mini games like shooting a three-pointer. Justine Moore of a16z had Argon build an interactive museum of Apple computers from scraped archival photos and 50 years of specs, the kind of project that goes viral on X, TikTok, and Instagram.

3. Teaching Argon My Voice 

I asked Argon to study my X posts, newsletters, and YouTube videos and turn them into a skill. It built a skill package with a core voice operating system, sentence rhythm rules, a lexicon of terms I coined, and verbatim samples and templates. Its post on marketing engineers covered micro products over PDF lead magnets and tweet-sized landing pages, signed off with "Be well, Greg," and earned a 9.2 out of 10 from me, which makes Argon probably the best frontier model for writing right now.

4. Vibe Manufacturing on Shopify Argon built me a Vibe Manufacturing Studio, an embeddable Shopify widget that shows print time, material cost, and suggested retail price, then exports a print-ready STL file. The file goes to a Bambu Lab printer, or to the Slant 3D print-on-demand API for anyone who'd rather skip owning printers. A custom espresso portafilter station shows the demand signal, since r/espresso members spend $2,500 on machines and gladly pay $49 for one.

5. Free Tools From Boring SaaS 

The "SaaS is over" crowd is mostly indie hackers selling to indie hackers, and most people gladly pay for software that makes life easier. I find recurring, boring problems on G2, Capterra, Reddit, and Idea Browser, then give away a focused tool to that buyer. My test prompt asked Antigravity for a quoting app that turns a commercial cleaning company's site visit notes into a reviewed price proposal, and it nailed the engineering on prompt one.

6. Six Techniques and Pricing 

I use /plan to agree on scope, /subagents to run research in parallel, /goal for higher quality, /browser to test the user journey, /learn to turn corrections into project rules, and high effort as my default after a start on medium. I tested on Google AI Ultra at $100 a month, which includes the Antigravity app, the CLI, and up to 1 million output tokens, while the $19.99 Pro plan suits text generation and web search. I close with my rule to marry the niche and date the product.

snippet.title: 8 GitHub Repos To Go Viral and Make Money
snippet.description:
In this solo episode, I walk through eight GitHub repos and AI skills that I test at night and on weekends. The list covers launch videos, social research, local voice and dubbing, editable decks, agent teams, lead-magnet tools, idea stress-testing, and design guidance. For each one, I explain what it does, how I'd set it up, and one concrete way to use it to make money or run a business more easily. Most are free to download, and you pay for the model you run them with.

Timestamps

00:00 – Intro
01:25 – Brag: Launch Videos From a Link
04:50 – Agent Reach for Customer Research
07:46 – Voice Studio: Local AI Voice and Dubbing
10:41 – PPT Master: Editable Decks From Notes
12:59 – OpenRig: Coding Agents as a Team
14:57 – Free Tools Skill by Corey Haynes
17:25 – Grill Me Skill by Matt Pocock
19:31 – Impeccable: Design Guidance for Agents
23:03 – My Top Picks: Brag and Agent Reach
24:07 – Closing Thoughts

GitHub Repo Links:
Brag: https://startup-ideas-pod.link/brag
Agent Reach: https://startup-ideas-pod.link/agent-reach
Voice Studio: https://startup-ideas-pod.link/voice-studio
PPT Master: https://startup-ideas-pod.link/ppt-master
OpenRig: https://startup-ideas-pod.link/openrig
Free Tool: https://startup-ideas-pod.link/marketing-skills
Grill Me Skill: https://startup-ideas-pod.link/grill-me
Impeccable Skill: https://startup-ideas-pod.link/impeccable

Key Points

• Most of these tools are free to download, and the main cost is the model you run them with.
• Work I do for someone up front, like a launch video or a design fix, starts a conversation in place of a cold email.
• Posts on Reddit, X, and YouTube show tasks people still do by hand, and a small tool can fix them.
• Translated onboarding videos make a recurring monthly service for other companies.
• Grill Me logs my assumptions so I check them with a real customer before I build.
• Ten clients at $1,000 a month is $10,000 a month, and that cash flow funds the move from services to technology.

Numbered Section Summaries

1. Brag

I start with Brag, a skill that turns your project or a website link into a short launch video with music, motion, and post copy. I use Brag Slim, which is designed for Opus 5.5. You pick vertical, square, or landscape and redo any scene that feels off.

2. Agent Reach

Agent Reach sets up the tools your agent needs to research a topic across YouTube, Reddit, and X. I use it for customer research. I search phrases like "I export it," "I copy this into," and "does anyone know a workaround," then talk to the people behind the posts.

3. Voice Studio
Voice Studio is a desktop app for AI voice work, similar to 11 Labs. It runs local models on your own hardware, so a faster computer helps. It generates speech, works from a recording of your own voice, and dubs video into other languages. I'd start with a short recording of myself, then translate the tutorials behind the three most common support questions, with a fluent speaker checking the result.

4. PPT Master

PPT Master turns documents or notes into an editable presentation, and it accepts your own company template. I'd test it first on a proposal I already wrote, with the private information removed, so I know what a good result looks like.

5. OpenRig

OpenRig organizes coding agents into a team, so one agent builds a change, another checks it, and the work passes between them. It works with Codex and Claude Code, runs on Mac or Linux with Node and Tmux, and changes some agent settings, so read those before you run it.

6. Free Tools 

Free Tools is a skill from Corey Haynes's marketing collection. It helps you work out what to build and give away to attract the right customers. A skill is a reusable set of instructions for your agent, sometimes with scripts and examples, so you stop rewriting giant prompts every time.

7. Grill Me

Grill Me, a skill by Matt Pocock, interviews you about an idea or decision in rounds and follows up on your answers. I'd use it before I build something I'm excited about, because that's when I skip the awkward questions.

8. Impeccable

Impeccable, built by Paul Bakaus, gives coding agents specific design guidance once you tell it who the product is for. It has commands like critique, polish, bolder, and quieter. I'd run critique on a page

In this episode, I talk with Vas from Varick about what it takes to put AI to work inside a real company. Vas makes the case that AI pays off through process reengineering, and he walks me through the exact method his forward deployed engineers (FDEs) use: interviews, process mining, step sorting, and agents built inside existing systems of record. We go through real engagements, including a $5B public software company and an accounts payable overhaul that cut the cost per invoice from $31 to $6. By the end, you get a clear picture of the FDE role, the business opportunity behind AI roll-ups, and a five-day plan to start on your own.

snippet.title: OpenAI DevDay: Dots, Agents & $100B Opportunities
snippet.description:
I watched almost 60 minutes of Sam Altman on stage at OpenAI Dev Day 2026. Out of 20-plus launches, I pick the three or four that I think can make people billions of dollars in aggregate. I break down Dots, OpenAI's personal agent platform, plus the Decisions API, the Agents API with computer use, and Sign in with ChatGPT. I also share my four-step framework for building in this world and two business ideas I hope someone takes. If you want to build a business and make money around AI, this episode is for you.

Timestamps

00:00 – Intro
01:48 – Dots, the Personal Agent Platform
03:29 – OpenAI Doubles Down on Plugins
05:02 – Decisions API
06:43 – Agents API With Computer Use
08:01 – Sign In With ChatGPT
12:36 – Where should you build?
13:46 – Idea: Real-World Work APIs
15:04 – Idea: Analytics for Agent Discovery
17:05 –Closing Thoughts

Key Points

• Dots gives plugin builders a front door to 1.2 billion weekly active users.
• OpenAI is doubling down on plugins to make ChatGPT the app ecosystem for AI.
• Sign in with ChatGPT lets users bring their current plan, so a free core app with paid upsells now works.
• Workflows too niche for OpenAI to build become viable businesses.
• The strongest businesses in this world own the trigger, the action, and the feedback.
• Two open opportunities: real-world work APIs and an analytics layer for agent discovery

Numbered Section Summaries

1. The Launches Worth Your Attention

OpenAI shipped 20-plus features at Dev Day 2026, and I focus on four: Dots, the Decisions API, the Agents API, and Sign in with ChatGPT. I cover GPT 6.1 Soul, Ultrafast, Private Intelligence, and Spaces briefly at the end.

2. Dots and the Plugin Comeback

Dots is OpenAI's answer to Muse by Meta and Instinct. A user asks for help, like fixing a permit or finding a restaurant, ChatGPT understands the job, and it selects a plugin, which is essentially a mini app. By my paraphrase, Sam admitted plugins got mixed reviews before, and now he plans to make them a thing. I think billions of dollars of transactions will flow through personal agent platforms, and maybe trillions over 10 to 20 years.

3. Decisions API, OpenAI's Answer to Jev

The Decisions API is in limited preview. It focuses Luna's intelligence on user-defined questions with finite, predefined answers, so developers can classify content, route requests, or choose an agent's next action. I'm hooked on Jev, and I see UI design as an underserved use case, like finding the highest-converting app store screenshots and direct response websites.

4. Agents API and Vertical Harnesses

The Agents API now supports computer use and brings Codex's multi-agent capabilities, tool search, tool calling, and context compaction into your application. OpenAI runs the infrastructure. If you have great data, a great brand, or deep knowledge of a vertical, I would be playing with this today.

5. Sign In With ChatGPT and Free Core Apps

Users can now sign in with their ChatGPT login and use their token allowance on other websites. I compare it to Facebook login, which helped create billion-dollar companies like Yelp. People hesitate to pay $20 or $30 a month for another AI app, so I would make the core app free and charge for enterprise features, team sharing, and more data. Before, the builder paid for inference, which made a free core app hard.

6. Sell Workflows Over Tokens

Tiny AI categories are now economically viable, like an agent that cleans architectural CAD files, a researcher that monitors one scientific field, a Shopify catalog cleanup desktop app, a video tool built around one editing workflow, or a contract review tool for one type of franchise agreement. The value comes from proprietary information, a specialist workflow, access to outside systems, collaboration and auditability, a network of humans or suppliers, and a measurable business result.

7. Trigger, Decision, Action, Feedback

My framework starts with a trigger, like an invoice coming due, inventory running low, or tax time. ChatGPT decides what to do next, an application takes the action, and feedback shows whether it was approved or rejected. The strongest businesses will own the trigger, the action, and the feedback.

snippet.title: $5T opportunity: AI Roll Ups
snippet.description:
In this solo episode, I break down the $5 trillion wave of small businesses set to change hands as their owners retire, and why AI agents make this wave a real opening for solo founders. I walk through how Thrive Holdings and General Catalyst buy accounting firms, property managers, and support centers, then run AI agents inside them to lift margins. Then I show how I'd run a one-person holding company: the folder structure, the agent files, the human approval rule, and my average week. I close with the strongest arguments against AI roll-ups, including the one I take most seriously.

Timestamps

00:00 – Intro
01:52 – Why the $5 Trillion Shift Is Happening Now
04:52 – Examples: Thrive Holdings& General Catalyst
08:38 – The Fund Playbook
10:07 – The Small-Deal Gap
10:51 – The One-Person Holdco
14:23 – The Folder Structure
16:47 – The Agent Pipeline
18:38 – Inside a Reviewer Agent File
19:41 – My Week Running the Holdco
21:49 – How to Land the First Business
22:24 – Arguments Against AI Roll-Ups
27:43 – Closing Thoughts

Key Points

• About a million small businesses, part of a $5 trillion shift, are set to sell by 2035 as owners retire (McKinsey).
• AI agents now handle the work these firms run on: data entry, document chasing, status updates, and first drafts.
• The big funds chase bigger deals, which leaves the small firms open for solo founders and small teams.
• A one-person holdco runs on shared agents and rules, plus a GM with real upside at each business.
• A person approves all agent work before it reaches a client.
• The corrections log, turned into rules every week, becomes the most valuable asset in the holdco.

Numbered Section Summaries

1. Why the $5 Trillion Shift Is Happening Now

Three things line up at once. Owners who built accounting practices, insurance agencies, and property management companies in the 80s and 90s want to retire, and their kids and employees often want something else. AI agents can now do the typing, chasing, and status updates well enough that a person only checks the draft, while buyers still price these firms at 5 to 10% profit.

2. What Thrive and General Catalyst Are Buying

Thrive Holdings has bought close to 50 accounting firms in 24 months, and at one of them, Larson Gross in Bellingham, Washington, AI built on OpenAI's Codex processed 7,000 returns this tax season while accountants saved 31% of their time on average. General Catalyst set aside $1.5 billion, and its company Long Lake reports 18 property management acquisitions and $100 million in EBITDA in under two years. Many of these numbers come from young companies raising money that have yet to face a recession, so I read them as a strong signal of direction and stop short of calling them proof.

3. The Fund Playbook and the Small-Deal Gap

The funds build the agents and software first, buy a trusted firm, run agents in the background, then move the back office over, so revenue holds while costs fall and margins can climb from 5 to 10% to 30 to 40% if the thesis holds. General Catalyst companies pay 60 to 70% in cash and the founder rolls about 30% into equity, which gives the person with the client relationships a reason to stay through the handoff. A billion-dollar fund skips a $2 million bookkeeping firm, most of the businesses up for sale sit at that size, and many retiring owners would rather hand their life's work to a person.

4. The One-Person Holdco

I sit at the top of a holding company that owns a few small businesses, each run by a GM who already works there and gets a real piece of the upside. Every business shares the same agents, rules, back office, and dashboards, so each new business is easier than the last. I use the same models the funds use, I do the integration myself, and after six years running my own holdco, I know the GM decides how far each business goes.

5. Folders, Agents, and the Human Approval Rule

The folder structure holds a thesis, a shared layer with global rules, test examples, and runbooks, and one folder per business with client, people, and rules files plus a corrections log. Work moves from an intake agent to a preparer agent to a reviewer agent, and the reviewer can block work while only a person sends it to the client. Each agent gets a plain-English job description that covers its job, its limits, and when to stop and ask a human.

snippet.title: Meta Muse AI Connectors: The App Store for AI?
snippet.description:
In this solo episode, I break down the huge business opportunity because Meta has opened Muse, its personal AI agent, to developers. You can now submit a connector, which lets Muse use your service when someone asks it for help, and I think this could be the app store moment for AI. I explain how a connector works, share four startup ideas you can build on one, and cover how to get customers beyond Meta's directory. I also show how I'd build a first version with a coding agent like Claude Code or Codex, and what I'd test before submitting it to Meta for review.

Timestamps

00:00 – Intro
01:35 – The App Store Parallel
04:55 – How a Muse Connector Works
07:29 – Startup Idea 1: Lead Gen for Business Suppliers
09:28 – Startup Idea 2: Home Repair Dispatch
11:07 – Startup Idea 3: Paddle Match and Court Finder
12:47 – Startup Idea 4: Family Dinner Planning
14:10 – How to pick an idea?
14:56 – How People Find Your Connector
15:32 – Growth Idea 1: Partner With Creators
16:17 – Growth Idea 2: Product-Led Sharing
17:46 – Growth Idea 3: Connected Marketplaces and Directory Placement
19:34 – Building the First Version
21:38 – Custom Connectors and Meta Approval
23:56 – Where to Start This Week
25:31 – Closing thoughts

Muse Connector Prompt: https://startup-ideas-pod.link/muse-connector-prompt

Key Points

• Meta has opened Muse to developers, and a connector lets Muse use your service when someone asks it for help.
• I look closely at the step in a request where someone needs a business that can deliver and money changes hands.
• With a small budget, I'd start with lead generation, because I can show a customer a sample before writing much software.
• I plan distribution around channels I can reach, such as creators, product-led sharing, and connected marketplaces.
• A coding agent can build the first version, and I still inspect the results and test the awkward requests myself.
• To start this week, I'd talk to one type of customer about the last time they dealt with the task.

Numbered Section Summaries

1. The App Store Moment for AI

Apple opened the App Store in 2008, and by June 2010 it had paid developers a billion dollars from paid apps and in-app purchases. Muse follows the same model, with Meta building the assistant and outside businesses supplying the services that complete a customer's request. As of recording, Muse is the number one app in the App Store.

2. Your Service in the Middle of a Request

Someone organizing a small event starts with a venue, later realizes they need to rent equipment, and an equipment rental company becomes relevant at that step. Meta now has a submission process, a directory of approved connectors, and editors who can feature them. An app store feature once brought me about 40,000 downloads a day for free, so being early can help you learn faster than others in your category.

3. How a Muse Connector Works

In my example, I ask Muse for a two-hour podcast studio on Tuesday afternoon with a $200 budget, the connector asks the studio's API for a room, and the service books it once I approve the $160 offer. Duffel already does this in travel, where its Muse integration lets people search flights and manage bookings, and the company has passed a billion dollars in annual transaction value. If you already have software, check what customers can do through your API today, because a useful connector might sit inside your product.

4. Custom Connectors, Review, and Open Questions

Meta documents a custom connector option, so I can connect my own Muse to a service through its API and test the integration before pursuing a public listing. Stacktree's founder published a firsthand account of the review form, which offers options for an API or an existing MCP server and asks for product information, usage examples, documentation, and support details. My open questions are how many users Muse will reach and how many connectors Meta will approve, and whether review will look like YC at 0.01% or like the Apple App Store.

- I estimate AI-native firms can reach 60%+ net margins, compared with 10–15% for a typical human agency.

- I built Studio Operator with six prompts, one layer of the firm per prompt, in a deliberate order.

- I match each job to a model: people, products, text, repairs, long scenes, speech, motion, or finishing.

- The strongest ideas pair a creative surface with a repetitive, checkable operational core.

Numbered Section Summaries

1. Three Shifts at Once

Creative models like Kling, Flux, and Seedream moved far past the AI Will Smith spaghetti video. Astra can read a messy brief, plan the work, pick specialist models, track budget, and repair failures. The Higgsfield API puts the models, pricing, requests, and outputs behind one API, which replaces a dozen separate accounts.

2. Human Agency vs. AI-Native Firm

A traditional creative agency grows through word of mouth and organic social, and it nets 10–15% because hiring, turnover, and marketing eat the margin. An AI-native firm adds marketplaces like Upwork and Fiverr as a third sales channel and takes on $100 to $25,000 jobs at gross margins that can reach 70–95%. I call it semi-autonomous: AI does the work, and a person approves it.

3. The Learning Loop

In a human agency, lessons walk out the door with the people who learned them. In an AI-native firm, every job feeds a loop that raises quality and margin, and I expect higher exit multiples because the business runs more like software.

4. Inside Studio Operator

My dashboard shows 25 active jobs, a $3,400 pipeline, and $3,200 in estimated gross profit. For a blood orange aperitif image, the client pays $10, Higgsfield production costs about one cent, and my expected profit is $9.99; the five-second video costs about $0.70 and includes a marketplace channel fee, which I put at 5–15%. Autonomy settings cap spend per job, repair cost, and attempts per step, and client memory stores logos, colors, fonts, and rejected styles for accounts like Moro Coffee.

5. A Model Primer by Job

Before I pick a model, I ask four questions: image, video, or speech; new asset or repair; cheap exploration or final version; and what must stay fixed. Then I route: Soul for people, Seedream or Flux for products, Ideogram or Recraft for text and layout, Qwen for repairs, Seedance for longer scenes, Kling for hero shots, Wan or Minimax for speech, Kling Motion Control for copied movement, and Topaz plus finishing tools for delivery.

6. Three Startup Ideas

An always-on ad studio sells a weekly creative pack for one SKU, with prospects from the Meta Ad Library and a $750–$1,500 paid sprint that grows into a monthly package. A franchise localization service turns one approved national campaign into local versions for brands with 20–200 locations, starting with a paid five-location pilot. An industrial catalog service turns spec sheets and CAD files into demos, training clips, and sales graphics, starting in one vertical with prospects from ThomasNet and trade show exhibitor lists.

snippet.title: $30M Writer: Never write AI slop again
snippet.description:
Get Your Complete Financial OS at https://startup-ideas-pod.link/brex_SIP

In this episode I speak with Nicolas Cole about the real value of everything you write on the internet. Cole has 15 years of experience as a nonfiction writer and ghostwriter, and he runs the SaaS platform Typeshare. He gives me a simple model with three tiers of content: commodity, personality, and original. He also explains the digital brain, which he calls your personal language model, and he shows how AI repeats your approved language at scale. By the end, you know how to judge the short, medium, and long-term value of a piece before you write it.

Make AI Sound like you: https://startup-ideas-pod.link/plm

Start Writing Online In 30 Days: https://startup-ideas-pod.link/ship30

Timestamps
00:00:00 – Intro
00:03:36 – POV is the Moat
00:05:40 – Language As Open Source
00:11:24 – Value Is Relative To The Reader
00:14:26 – Approved Language
00:17:43 – The Value of AI in Writing
00:22:09 – Commodity Ideas
00:24:23 – How To Set Up The System
00:27:58 – Ownership IS Association
00:33:56 – Build your Personal Data Set
00:39:53 – Branded Content vs Founder-Led Content
00:45:17 – What is Original Content?
00:46:35 – Writing Versus Short-Form Video
00:48:58 – Three Types of Hooks
00:49:50 – Timely Content vs Timeless Content
00:53:27 – Voice is 3 dialed settings
00:56:32 – Finding your Voice
01:00:49 – The Company Brain As The Moat
01:07:30 – Closing Thoughts

Key Points

• A point of view creates the moat, because copycats must wait for your next idea.
• Content sits in three tiers: commodity, personality, and original. Each tier adds different leverage.
• Ownership equals association. Volume builds it, and personality details make it strong.
• Your life story is the unmade data set, so AI learns it only from your own writing.
• Every piece sits on a spectrum from timely to timeless, so match your expectations to the type.
• Humans do the thinking and the writing. Robots do the repeating and the remixing.

Numbered Section Summaries

1. The Point Of View Moat

Cole answers the popular claim that AI removes the moat from SaaS. He says a moat appears when a product carries a method, such as Typeshare and its personal language model idea. A competitor who copies features must still look back at the person who does the thinking.
    
2. Language Is Open Source

Cole describes the alphabet, words, and most groupings of words as shared property. He uses the example of a health sentence that millions of people repeat. This explains why readers label some writing as AI slop: they recognize a commodity sentence.
    
3. The Three Tiers Of Content

Cole separates commodity content, personality content, and original content. Commodity content helps beginners, and it stays useful as a first step. Personality content and original content raise the long-term value of your library.
    
4. Approved Language And The Digital Brain

Cole spent a decade as a ghostwriter, where he assembled client language from books, blogs, and recorded meetings. He calls this approved language, and he sees AI as the automated version of the same job. A larger library gives you more net new combinations.
    
5. Ownership As Association

Cole defines ownership as association. Volume creates the first layer, and personality details create the second layer. I add Ramit Sedi and Dave Ramsey as two people who own opposite sides of the same commodity idea about coffee and savings.
    
6. The Unmade Data Set

Cole explains that everybody uses the same models and the same public data. Your formative experiences, mistakes, and life facts stay outside that data until you write them down. He gives the example of his World of Warcraft sentence, which he repeated in hundreds of pieces after one Quora answer went viral.
    
7. Timely Versus Timeless

Cole puts every piece on a spectrum. A meme captures 24 hours of attention, and an essay serves you for ten years. He asks one question before you start: how much value do you extract, and over what time horizon?

snippet.title: Jev is HERE. How to use it
snippet.description:
In this episode, I talk with Ryan Vogel about Jev, a new type of AI built for classification. Ryan shows how Jev takes an input plus an output schema and returns a probability for each choice in about 200 milliseconds. He demos Jev sorting 1,700 emails for 18 cents total, then covers lead scoring, support routing, video clipping, and browser control. I push him on the startup angle: find a business with an expensive queue of incoming information and put Jev at the front of it. You leave with a clear mental model, real use cases, and a simple way to try it today.

Links Mentioned: 

Jev/Typeface AI: https://typesafe.ai
AI Gateway: https://vercel.com/ai-gateway

Timestamps
00:00 – Intro
02:27 – What Jev Is and Why It Matters
04:32 – Email Triage Demo
07:19 – Jev as an AI Decision Maker
15:46 – How to Use Jev in a Business
20:48 – Startup Idea: Local Services Matching and Instant Quotes
22:51 – Use Case 1: Bitcoin Signal Test and Limits
24:03 – Use Case 2: Auto-Clipping Long Videos
25:27 – Use Case 3: Browser Control: Flight Pick in 7.1 Seconds
26:18 – How to Get Access
27:25 – Closing Thoughts

Key Points

• Jev is a classifier: an input and an output schema go in, and a probability for each choice comes out.
• Ryan's demo scores 1,700 emails for 18 cents total.
• Each Jev query takes about 200 milliseconds, whatever the input and output structure.
• Use Jev at any point where a business makes fast, repeatable decisions on incoming data.
• Keep Jev in an advisory role, and save frontier models for high-intelligence tasks like trading.
• Instant access runs through the Vercel Gateway, and a waitlist covers direct access.

Numbered Section Summaries

1. What Jev Actually Is

Ryan explains Jev as a classifier. You define an input and an output schema, and Jev returns a probability for each option, for example 80% orange, 10% red, and 10% blue for the color of an iPhone.

2. The 18-Cent Email Demo

Ryan runs Jev on 1,700 of his own emails and scores each one for category, priority, spam score, and reply likelihood. The run uses 4.2 million input tokens and 500,000 output tokens and costs 18 cents total.

3. A Decision Model, Distinct From a Chat Model

Jev returns only structured output, meaning the numbers and categories from your schema, with zero visible reasoning. Developers can drop that type-safe output straight into code. Ryan also tests Jev as a letter-by-letter text generator to show how a decision model differs from a chat model.

4. Cheap Enough to Experiment

A $5 intro credit lasts Ryan's team two days of heavy use, and he estimates $10 could last about three months. His girlfriend's graphic design agency uses Jev to score contact-form leads on a scale from 0 to 1, so high-value leads get a fast reply.

5. The AI Traffic Cop

I frame Jev as a traffic cop: information comes in, and Jev decides what it is, how important it is, and what happens next. A high-confidence lead goes to a human, a lower score goes to automation or an LLM, and the lowest scores get ignored. Ryan adds support routing, where 200-millisecond answers replace slow streaming responses.

6. Put Jev at the Front of the Queue

I ask how to find a business with an expensive queue of incoming information and put Jev at the front of it. Ryan describes a local services platform that matches a request like "I need my driveway power washed" to the best nearby business and turns "instant quote" forms into truly instant quotes.

7. Where Jev Struggles

Ryan's Bitcoin test, which asks Jev to buy, hold, or sell every minute, performs poorly. OpenAI's latest frontier model does a little better because it cross-references news. Ryan's advice: use Jev for routing-style decisions and keep it away from your portfolio.

8. Clips, Browser Control, and Getting Started

Ryan's video clipper scores 17 moments in about three seconds, and he builds it in about 10 minutes. A Browser Use demo shows Jev picking a flight from Zurich to London in 7.1 seconds. To start, use the Vercel Gateway and ask your AI agent which of your daily workflows could use a decision maker like Jev.

snippet.description:
Invites while they last to Instinct: https://startup-ideas-pod.link/instinct_ai

I sit down with Remy to go through Instinct, the new invite-only personal agent that runs inside iMessage. Remy shares his raw chat history on screen: a haircut booking in Copenhagen, a restaurant reservation, a Bali visa on arrival, and an Emirates Skywards sign-up. We cover the parts that impress us, the points where the agent hits a wall, and the privacy questions that stay open. By the end of this episode you understand what Instinct does today, and you get fresh ideas for personal agents in general.

Timestamps

00:00 – Intro
02:08 – Instinct Pros
11:18 – Instinct Cons
13:16 – Simple Onboarding
15:19 – Tools and Connectors
17:43 – Example 1: Booking a Haircut in Copenhagen
20:24 – Example 2: Restaurant Booking and Calendar Entry
23:03 – Example 3: Bali Visa on Arrival and Emirates Skywards
26:00 – Closing Thoughts

Key Points

• Instinct hides the agent complexity behind a phone number and iMessage, so a first-time user starts in seconds.
• Remy gets it to book a haircut, hold a restaurant table, file a Bali visa on arrival, and open an Emirates Skywards account.
• A spend-limited virtual card keeps the blast radius small when the agent pays for things.
• The agent stalls when a task needs a phone app or an Indonesian checkout page.
• Users report that Instinct keeps copies of email after they disconnect Google, so treat privacy as an open risk.
• The trusted person network lets one Instinct talk to another, which builds network effects into the agentic era.

Numbered Section Summaries

1. The Invite-Only Launch

Remy first sees Instinct on X, where large AI accounts talk about it. The site shows a wait list, so he grabs an invite code from a public tweet. Scarcity drives the curiosity, and Remy reads the rollout as a marketing play as much as a compute limit.
    
2. Onboarding Built for the Mass Market

Remy signs in with a phone number and lands straight in iMessage. The agent opens with photo examples: flight bookings, check-ins, smoothie orders, subscription cancellations. Remy teaches founders AI for a living, so he values a flow that skips MCPs, CLIs, and markdown files.
    
3. The Workspace, the Connectors, and the Vault

A simple web workspace sits beside the chat. It holds contact methods, connectors for email, Slack and Granola, and a vault for logins, cards, and addresses. Remy connects his email accounts and stays impressed by how much context Instinct pulls about him.
    
4. Real Tasks: Haircut, Restaurant, Visa

Remy asks for salons in Copenhagen. Instinct researches spots, pulls reviews, sends photos, emails the salon, and confirms the booking hours later. It then holds a table at Bistro Central, files the Bali visa on arrival and the arrival card, and opens an Emirates Skywards account with a saved password.
    
5. Human Touches: Reactions, Memory, and Game Pigeon

Instinct reacts to messages, reads a thumbs-up as approval, and uses loud effects and confetti. It recalls the monitor from an earlier chat and adds it to the visa arrival card. It even plays a round of Game Pigeon Cup Pong, which surprises us both.
    
6. Network Effects, Privacy, and the Ten-Billion Question

The founder Noah announces a trusted person network, so one Instinct can talk to another. I compare the invite rollout to Clubhouse in 2020, which raised at $4vbillion. Meanwhile Claire Vo and Peter Yang report that Instinct keeps copies of their email after they disconnect Google, and the terms raise the same flag.

snippet.title: Building a Software Factory that actually works (Full Course)
snippet.description:
Get Your Complete Financial OS at https://startup-ideas-pod.link/brex_SIP

I welcome Ras Mic back to the pod to explain the phrase "software factory." Mic shares his screen and walks through the exact system that he runs today. His factory has four steps: isolate, build, prove, and ship. He keeps the whole system in five or six markdown files, so it works with any model and any harness. By the end of this episode, you can boot up your own factory, run many agents in parallel, and trust the code that comes back.

Create your own Software Factory: https://startup-ideas-pod.link/ras-software-factory

Timestamps
00:00 – Intro
02:17 – Software Factory Definition
03:44 – Why the Software Factory Matters
05:23 – Step 1: Isolate With Git Work Trees
11:34 – Step 2: Build With the Code Structure Skill
14:48 – Step 3: Prove With Evidence-Driven Testing
22:25 – Step 4: Ship With Grep Loop and Greptile
26:52 – The Physical Factory Analogy
29:21 – A Software Factory Is Markdown Files
30:02 – Closing Thoughts

Key Points

• A software factory is a workflow of skills and domain knowledge, so it runs with any model and any harness.
• Isolate: every feature starts in a fresh git work tree branched from origin main, so each agent keeps its own station.
• Build: a code structure skill makes the agent write service layer code that a human developer can read.
• Prove: the agent records a before state and an after state as video, screenshots, or numbers.
• Ship: Greptile scores the PR, and the agent loops back to build until it earns five out of five.
• Mic runs up to 15 features in parallel and reviews the visual proof instead of the raw code.

Numbered Section Summaries

1. What a Software Factory Means

Ras defines the term as a workflow, a set of skills, and domain knowledge, packed into markdown files. The word "factory" points to structure, speed, and a conveyor belt that keeps quality high. He is clear that a software factory is a method rather than a product you buy.
    
2. Why the Factory Matters Now

Model intelligence keeps rising, and Ras names GPT-6 Astra as his workhorse and the model with the lowest hallucination rate. A factory lets you use that intelligence in a systematic way, instead of typing back and forth with a chat window. He offers his own skills for free, and he asks people to understand the process first and then adapt it.
    
3. The Agents.md File as the Master Instruction

The agents.md file is a single markdown document that goes into the agent chat ahead of every message. Ras says most people fill it with facts the agent already reads from the code base. He fills his with a workflow instead, because the workflow is the part the agent lacks.
    
4. Step 1: Isolate

A skill called "new feature" starts each task in a fresh git work tree branched from origin main. A work tree acts like a copy of the app, and the agent merges it back later. This keeps two agents apart, so one agent leaves the other agent's files alone. Michael shows four terminal tabs running four features on the same app.
    
5. Step 2: Build

The code structure skill tells the agent to write in a service layer architecture. Models get the job done, and they often get it done in a sloppy way, so the skill supplies the guideline. The result stays readable for a hired developer, for Michael, and for any fresh agent that opens the code base later.
    
6. Step 3: Prove

Two skills handle proof: evidence-driven testing and before and after. The agent records the broken state, does the work, and records the working state, then embeds both in the PR. When the after shot shows a gap, the agent sends itself back to the build step on its own. For work with an invisible surface, such as performance, the agent supplies numbers: one page went from 815 milliseconds to about 61.
    
7. Step 4: Ship

The grep loop skill sends the PR to Greptile, a third-party code review agent, and Greptile returns feedback plus a confidence score. A three out of five sends the agent back through build, prove, and ship. Ras steps in at five out of five and clicks merge. He mentions Code Rabbit and Macroscope as alternatives.
    
8. The Factory Analogy and the Case for Code Review

I map the four steps onto a real factory: a custom order gets its own station, the assembly line builds it, quality control tests it, and shipping sends it out the door. Ras agrees, and he says he may rename his skills to match.
